title: The nucleus is spherical because it is an immiscible fluid drop under uniform tension

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The nucleus is spherical because it is an immiscible fluid drop under uniform tension

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The nucleus is almost always spherical because its fluid substance does not mix with the surrounding protoplasm, so it is bounded by a film of uniform surface tension and immersed in a medium transmitting uniform fluid pressure; where the cytoplasm becomes more solid (as in muscle cells or mucus-laden epithelial cells) the pressure becomes unsymmetrical and the nucleus is deformed.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: So long as the fluid substance of the nucleus is qualitatively different from, and incapable of mixing with, the fluid or semi-fluid protoplasm which surrounds it, we shall expect it to be, as it almost always is, of spherical form.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter IV, “On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell”; topic “Form of the resting nucleus”. Scope: nuclei of cells generally; contrasted with muscle and epithelial cells with stiffened cytoplasm

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch04-03: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Shape and mechanical predictors are measurable, and extensive public cell images permit broad correlational and some perturbational tests. Full discrimination of an immiscible-drop mechanism from envelope and chromatin mechanics needs variables absent from many datasets.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure nuclear sphericity, cytoplasmic rheology, external stress anisotropy, and nuclear-envelope tension across cell types and perturbations. Support requires round nuclei in fluid isotropic surroundings and predictable deformation as surrounding stiffness or pressure anisotropy increases.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Nuclear lamina and chromatin mechanics provide plausible alternative causes.

Most image datasets lack matched cytoplasmic rheology or pressure.

fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Nuclear outline versus cell type is directly measurable in public images, and muscle versus soft-cell comparisons match the contrast Thompson draws. The immiscible-film mechanism is not in those images: lamina mechanics produce the same deformations. The shape correlation is therefore a partial test of the claim, strongest as a description and weaker as a force law.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure nuclear roundness against cytoplasmic stiffness or solidity across cell types, including muscle and secretory epithelia. Nuclei that are spherical in fluid cytoplasm and systematically deformed where the cytoplasm is stiffened would support the claim; spherical nuclei inside stiffened cytoplasm, or deformed nuclei in uniform fluid cytoplasm, would refute the pressure account.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The nuclear lamina and chromatin packing deform nuclei without a change in cytoplasmic fluidity.

Image archives rarely include a stiffness measurement for the same cell.

Roundness is compatible with an interfacial film and with a tense cortical shell.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.5
analysis feasibility: 0.6
data adequacy: 0.5
data existence: 0.65
operationalizability: 0.7
